speaker_role: independent counselor (SupertutorTV, ~20 years coaching students into top-10/top-20 colleges)
commercial_incentive: Yes - promotes her own coaching service at supertutortv.com
key_insights: A student with only two formal activities got into a top-10 school ED by building a deep, problem-focused personal narrative instead of a long activity list
Coach argues the most powerful application element is identifying a real-world problem and pursuing a self-directed solution path, not signing up for 'clipboard' clubs
Recommends framing interests around a problem to solve (e.g., methane capture) rather than a self-focused trait (e.g., 'I'm good at math')
Freshmen/sophomores have time to build unique, 'N of one' projects (research, apps, advocacy) that read as unlike anyone else's application
Test scores and grades are described as a baseline requirement, not a differentiator, for top-10/20 applicants
Claims roughly half of top-20 schools are test-required and that trend is increasing (cites Princeton reinstating by 2027)
States UC schools are SAT/ACT-blind but still consider AP scores in admissions per the coach's reading of UC's own site
Recommends near-zero B's, no C's, mostly 4s/5s on APs, and calculus if possible for top-10/20 aspirants
specific_numbers_or_facts: Coach states ~44% of American high school students have an A average / ~3.5+ unweighted GPA
Coach states about 50% of top-20 ranked colleges are test-required, with Princeton adding itself by 2027 (11/20 schools)
Coach recommends 1550+ SAT or 35+ ACT to 'open all doors' for top-10/20 schools
Coach recommends no more than two B's and zero C's on transcript for top-10/20 applicants
Coach says she has had two students with perfect scores admitted to Stanford in the last five years
notable_or_distinctive: Frames the single most powerful admissions lever as an outward-facing 'problem to solve' narrative rather than self-focused interest ('I'm good at science'), illustrated with a specific low-activity-count admit story.
reliability_notes: All claims are the coach's personal opinion/experience with her own client base (small, selection-biased sample skewed toward highly qualified students), and stats like the 44% figure and test-required percentages are stated without citation; strong sales framing toward the end.
